items.title: Default virtual sticks are too dim to read at a glance
items.what: On the main fight screens (e.g., 390x844 gameplay shots), the stance/technique pads in the bottom third use very dark rings and faint arrow glyphs that nearly blend into the brown background; the directional chevrons are only slightly lighter than the panel behind them.
items.why: In a touch-first game, players must instantly understand where and how to drag. Low affordance on the primary controls causes hesitation and input errors in the first seconds of play.
items.how: Increase contrast of the stick UI in default mode: brighten outer ring/arrow strokes by ~25–35%, add a subtle inner glow or lighter plate behind arrows, and keep an always-visible active zone boundary. Preserve the warm palette, but separate luminance from the background.

items.title: Playable action is vertically squeezed by UI stack
items.what: In portrait gameplay, fighters occupy a narrow middle band while the lower half is dominated by instruction strip + two large sticks + labels. The action zone feels compressed between the top HUD and bottom controls.
items.why: Small on-screen fighters make reads (range, kick height, contact) harder, which directly hurts timing gameplay and perceived responsiveness.
items.how: Rebalance vertical layout: reduce joystick diameter and dead padding between instruction strip and sticks, collapse duplicate text labels, and move the camera/framing so fighters render ~10–15% larger during rounds.

items.title: Key combat guidance text is too small for phone readability
items.what: The command hints in the strip above the sticks (e.g., "◄ step ▲ jump" / "◄ reverse ► forward") are very small and tightly spaced; similarly, tags like "IN 2" inside the Fight button are tiny.
items.why: Players can’t reliably parse move mapping under time pressure, especially on 390px-wide screens, increasing early churn from confusion rather than challenge.
items.how: Bump critical instructional typography one size tier (and line height), reduce tracking on small caps, and simplify each side to 2–3 highest-value hints. For countdown chips, enlarge text and increase contrast against the gold button.

items.title: Fighters look slightly pasted over the mat
items.what: Across multiple combat shots, feet contact lacks convincing local shadowing and the sprite edges (especially around gi and hair) show mild cutout/fringe against the dojo background, making characters feel detached from the floor plane.
items.why: This weakens hit believability and the premium visual impression, especially in a game selling cinematic dojo atmosphere.
items.how: Add stronger dynamic contact shadows under each foot/stance center, plus subtle ambient occlusion decals tied to pose. Tighten sprite alpha edges (premultiplied-alpha cleanup/defringe) and apply a tiny color-match pass so edges inherit scene warmth.

items.title: Boot/loading progress indicator is too subtle
items.what: On the ShoeMoney loading screen, the progress bar is a very thin, low-contrast line near the lower middle; at a glance it reads almost like a divider, not a progress state.
items.why: First impression quality suffers when users can’t tell if the game is actively loading or stalled, increasing bounce risk before gameplay even starts.
items.how: Thicken the bar and raise contrast (track + fill), add a clear percentage or staged status text beneath "Downloading the game," and animate fill updates with short eased steps to signal activity.
